walk verb

go on foot

also walking, go for a walk, take a walk, on foot, go on foot, stroll, would you like to take a stroll?, hike, walk up and down

ambulō, ambulāre, ambulāvī, ambulātum

verb, first conjugation · Conjugation on Wiktionary

The everyday verb for walking, as against sitting, standing or running, and for walking about for exercise. “Go for a walk” is the supine with īre: ambulātum īre (Cic. Leg. 1.14, as Lewis & Short reads it), deambulātum īre (Cato in Cic. de Or. 2.256).

Other words

  • pedibus īre — go on foot, walk (not ride or drive)

    phrase · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 34: cum ingressus iter pedibus sit (Lewis & Short); Liv. 26.19 (Lewis & Short)

    Also pedibus venīre, proficīscī: on foot, as against on horseback or by carriage.

  • inambulō, inambulāre — walk up and down, pace about

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 6.2.5; Liv. 23.43.8 (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

  • deambulō, deambulāre, deambulāvī, deambulātum — take a stroll, walk about

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Cato Agr. 127 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 403; Traupman 54 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Rare (Lewis & Short). Short de- before a vowel, as Lewis & Short marks it (dĕambulo), against Traupman’s dēambulāre.

  • spatior, spatiārī, spatiātus sum — take a walk, stroll about

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 59: cum resideret, deinde spatiārētur (Lewis & Short); Traupman 108 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

Examples

  • nam ut tibi ambulandum, ungendum, sīc mihi dormiendum.

    for as you must walk and oil yourself, so I must sleep.Cic. Att. 9.7.7

  • Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem.

    They say that when Socrates was walking hard until evening and was asked why he did it, he answered that he was buying in hunger by walking, so as to dine better.Cic. Tusc. 5.97

  • Parā tē, ut eāmus ambulātum.

    Get ready, so that we can go for a walk.Cord. Coll. 1.24 (one transcription only)

  • Velīsne spatiārī?

    Would you like to take a stroll?Traupman 108

  • Deinde ego et amīcae deambulāmus.

    Then my friends and I go for a walk.Traupman 40

  • deambulātum īre

    to go for a walkTraupman 403

See also walk, run, walk the dog, go, path, stick.
